channel.title: Shubham Singh | Software Engineer
channel.description: SDE II at Amazon building production agentic AI systems and distributed infrastructure on AWS.

item.title: Delete more features
item.description: Shipping a feature has never been cheaper. Keeping one alive costs exactly what it always did. As generation gets faster, the scarce skill on a product team stops being the ability to add things and becomes the discipline to take them away.

item.title: Driftboard: rebuilding a Kanban board around drag that does not flicker
item.description: I had a small Kanban project built on a drag-and-drop library that Atlassian has since archived. Rebuilding it into Driftboard, a local-first board with rich cards and a command palette, came down to three decisions: which drag library to trust, how to make cross-column dragging stop flickering, and how to keep undo honest when every interaction mutates the board. Here is how each one went.

item.title: Jotdown: sticky notes with a real editor underneath
item.description: Apple Stickies is the most frictionless note app on the Mac and the least useful once a note grows past a grocery list. I wanted to keep the friction and fix the ceiling: floating desktop notes that are still one keystroke away, but with a real live-markdown editor inside each one. Here is how Jotdown is built, and the two decisions that made it possible.

item.title: Michi: building a trip planner that starts with the map
item.description: Most trip planners hand you a list, but the first question a trip actually raises is spatial: where are these places relative to each other, and can I do them in one afternoon? Michi answers that by making the map the interface and letting an AI itinerary hang off it. Here is how it is built, from the request contract to the photos.

item.title: One line a day: building a journal small enough to survive
item.description: Every journaling habit I ever started died of ambition. So I built One Line: a journal that accepts exactly one sentence and one mood per day, stores everything in the browser, and marbles a year of entries into ink on paper. The constraint is the product; everything else followed from it.

item.title: Local-first AI is personal computing, again
item.description: The most personal dataset ever assembled about you is your AI context: what you asked, what you saved, what you decided. The default architecture sends all of it to someone else's computer. Local-first AI is not a privacy hobby; it is the personal computer argument, replayed.

item.title: The disappearing junior engineer
item.description: AI agents are best at exactly the work junior engineers used to learn on. The industry is responding by hiring fewer juniors, which is a rational decision for every individual team and a catastrophic one for the profession. Where do the seniors of 2032 come from?

item.title: The web is being rebuilt for agents
item.description: A growing share of your site's visitors cannot see your CSS, will never watch your ad, and read your entire page in forty milliseconds. The web is quietly splitting into a human surface and a machine surface, and most teams are only designing for one of them.

item.title: Verification is the new bottleneck
item.description: AI collapsed the cost of producing code, prose, images, and answers. It did not collapse the cost of trusting them. That asymmetry is quietly restructuring every knowledge profession, and it explains where the real engineering work in AI systems has gone.

item.title: Shipping a local-first AI memory CLI
item.description: What Waymark taught me about building AI memory for personal agents: privacy is an architecture constraint, memory needs a data model, citations beat fluency, and release engineering is part of product trust.

item.title: How I rendered 50k agent spans at 60fps
item.description: A trace viewer for LLM agents has to draw tens of thousands of spans and stay smooth while you pan, zoom, and scrub. Here is the rendering pipeline that gets there - structure-of-arrays geometry, a segment-tree cull, level-of-detail, a decoupled render loop, and off-main-thread parsing.

item.title: Idempotency: the under-loved primitive
item.description: Retries are not an edge case. They are the normal operating condition of any distributed system. Idempotency is the property that makes retries safe, and it is the difference between at-least-once delivery and a customer charged twice.

item.title: TypeScript at the API boundary: contracts that do not lie
item.description: TypeScript types are erased at runtime. At the edges of your system, where data crosses a network or a process boundary, the type is a claim nobody is checking. Here is how to make those claims true instead of hopeful.

item.title: Why internal tools feel worse than consumer apps
item.description: Internal tools are often built for delivery, not use. The result is software with real business value, captive users, weak ownership, and a surprising amount of avoidable pain.

item.title: The hidden engineering behind citations in RAG systems
item.description: Citations in RAG systems are not a formatting detail. They are an engineering contract between retrieval, generation, rendering, auditability, and user trust.

item.title: Choosing analytics for a personal portfolio
item.description: A small engineering decision note on picking analytics for a portfolio site: what to measure, what not to overbuild, and why Microsoft Clarity is a practical fit when the goal is understanding visitor behavior.

item.title: Designing interfaces for agentic systems
item.description: Agentic products need interfaces for supervision, correction, evidence, and safe control. A practical guide to designing UI surfaces for systems that plan, call tools, revise artifacts, and sometimes need to stop.

item.title: Writing an HLD that survives cross-team review
item.description: Most high-level design documents are skimmed, signed, and forgotten. The ones that survive are written for specific readers, not a generic reviewer. Here is what changes when you take that seriously.

item.title: Error isolation for batch pipelines: when fail-fast is wrong
item.description: Standard data-engineering advice says validate strictly, fail loudly, and replay. That advice is wrong for any pipeline where one bad record cannot be allowed to block the run. Here is the pattern that replaces it.

item.title: The schema problem in LLM outputs
item.description: Structured output from LLMs is treated as a solved problem. It is not. The JSON looks right, but the contract underneath is fragile in ways that only show up under volume. Here is what actually has to be true at the boundary.

item.title: Agentic systems, explained from first principles
item.description: A plain-English map of agents, tools, MCP servers, streaming responses, agent frameworks, runtime infrastructure, memory, state, and the engineering choices that make agentic systems production-ready.

item.title: Human feedback is not a chat message
item.description: In production agent systems, human feedback should be modeled as a structured state transition, not appended to a conversation transcript.

item.title: What production agents need that demos do not
item.description: The gap between an impressive agent demo and a trustworthy production system is not model intelligence. It is state, tools, evals, permissions, observability, retries, and human feedback design.

item.title: Hybrid retrieval at scale: BM25 + kNN tradeoffs
item.description: When to reach for vector search, when keyword retrieval still wins, and the architectural decisions behind a citation-grounded compliance Q&A system.

item.title: From chained Lambdas to Step Functions
item.description: A migration retrospective: why brittle orchestration patterns fail at scale, how Map states unlocked per-marketplace parallelism, and what we would do differently.
